match.reason: The bank point on industry sectors classifies businesses by what they do, which is a different idea from the five-sector circular flow of money and goods between households, businesses, government, financial institutions and the overseas sector.

draft.title: The five-sector circular flow
card: The circular flow shows how money moves around an economy. The five sectors are households, businesses, government, financial institutions and the overseas sector.
money that leaves the flow of spending on local goods and services. They are saving (into financial institutions), tax (to government) and imports (to the overseas sector).
money that enters the flow. They are investment (businesses borrow from financial institutions to buy capital goods), government spending and exports (overseas buyers paying local businesses).
If injections are greater than leakages, spending in the economy rises. If leakages are greater than injections, it falls.
draft.remember: Saving, tax and imports leave the flow. Investment, government spending and exports enter it.

a.q: Which of these is an injection into the circular flow?
opts: A Victorian winery sells wine to buyers in Japan
A household puts part of its pay into a savings account
A shop buys a shipment of clothes made in Vietnam
A business pays company tax to the government
a.why: Exports bring money from the overseas sector to local businesses, so they are an injection. Saving is a leakage into financial institutions, and buying imports and paying tax are also leakages.
a.clue: Which one brings money in from outside the country?

b.q: Mia, a Geelong café owner, pays more tax and buys more imported coffee machines, while exports and investment stay the same. What is the likely effect on spending in the economy?
opts: It falls, because leakages rise and injections stay the same
It rises, because tax and imports add money to the flow
It stays the same, because tax goes back to government
It rises, because imported machines raise investment
b.why: Tax and imports are both leakages. If leakages rise while injections stay the same, leakages exceed injections and spending falls. The tax is not a net addition, because the card counts it as money leaving the flow of spending.
b.clue: Are tax and imports leakages or injections?

a.best: A Victorian winery sells wine to buyers in Japan

b.best: It falls, because leakages rise and injections stay the same

problems.detail: Mia buying more coffee machines for her café is buying capital goods, which the card defines as investment. Yet the question says investment stays the same. Students who apply the card's definition may be confused, or may find option d plausible.

The question holds exports and investment constant but says nothing about government spending, which is the third injection. If the government spends the extra tax, leakages need not exceed injections. That makes 'It stays the same, because tax goes back to government' arguable. State that government spending also stays the same.

Investment is described as businesses borrowing from financial institutions to buy capital goods. This implies investment is always funded by borrowing, when businesses can also use their own funds. Consider 'often by borrowing' or similar.

check.summary: Question b is muddled. Buying coffee machines is itself investment, which clashes with 'investment stays the same', and the question leaves government spending unstated, so leakages need not exceed injections. The card also implies investment is always funded by borrowing.
